title: The Olympic Games Through Time
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The Olympic Games are the largest sporting event in the world, watched by billions of people and attended by more than ten thousand athletes from over two hundred countries. Yet the modern Games are the revival of a very old tradition, and many of their customs, from the torch to the motto, show the influence of the past. The story of the Games is also a story about how attitudes have changed: who is allowed to compete, what counts as a sport and what the Games are for. This passage looks at three periods: the ancient Games, the revival in the nineteenth century and the Games of today.

The first Games, according to tradition, were held in 776 BC at Olympia, in southern Greece, and they were repeated every four years for nearly twelve centuries. They were held in honour of Zeus, the king of the gods, and they were as much a religious festival as a sporting contest. At first the only event was a short foot race; later the programme grew to include wrestling, boxing, chariot racing and the pentathlon. The competitors were free men, who trained for months and took an oath to compete fairly, and the winners received not gold but a wreath of olive leaves. Even so, their cities honoured them as heroes.

A remarkable feature of the ancient Games was the sacred truce. Before each festival, messengers travelled across the Greek world to announce that all wars must stop, so that athletes and spectators could travel safely to Olympia and home again. The truce was not always obeyed, but it was respected for centuries, and the idea that sport can create a pause in conflict is still part of the Olympic ideal. Women were not allowed to compete, and married women were forbidden to watch, though a separate festival for women, in honour of the goddess Hera, was held there.

The ancient Games ended around the year 393 AD, when a Christian emperor banned pagan festivals. They were forgotten for fifteen hundred years, until a French nobleman, Pierre de Coubertin, became convinced that sport could improve education and promote peace. He organised a congress, and in 1896 the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, with about two hundred and fifty athletes from fourteen nations, all of them men. The marathon was added, inspired by the legend of a messenger who ran from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens, and its victory by a Greek runner made the crowd wild with joy.

The Games grew steadily. Women first competed in 1900, in tennis and golf, and their number has increased until, at recent Games, they have made up nearly half of all athletes. The first Winter Games were held in Chamonix, France, in 1924, for sports on snow and ice. In 1960, in Rome, the first Paralympic Games were held for athletes with disabilities, and since then they have grown into a major event of their own, held in the same city shortly after the Olympics. Each Games has added new events, from beach volleyball to skateboarding, to attract young audiences.

The Games are rich in symbols. The five interlocking rings, designed by Coubertin, stand for the five inhabited continents as they were then understood, and the colours, together with the white background, include at least one colour from the flag of every nation. The motto, in Latin, is Citius, Altius, Fortius, which means Faster, Higher, Stronger. The torch is lit in Olympia by the rays of the sun and carried by relay to the host city, a custom introduced in 1936. At the opening ceremony the athletes march behind their national flags, and at the end of each event the national anthem of the winner is played.

Not everyone is pleased with the modern Games. Dr Helen Brandt, a sports historian, notes that the cost of hosting the Games has risen enormously, and that several cities have been left with empty stadiums that are expensive to maintain. There have also been scandals about doping and corruption. Yet she believes that the Games remain valuable. They give athletes a goal that inspires them to train for years, and they give ordinary people a rare moment in which countries compete without violence. She suggests that future Games should use existing buildings and be shared between several cities, to reduce costs and waste.
